reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Ludwig angina is a rapidly spreading cellulitis of the floor of the mouth involving the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces bilaterally
The great majority arise from dental infection, especially of the lower molar teeth whose roots relate to the mylohyoid line
It produces a tense, brawny, tender swelling of the upper neck and floor of mouth that does not usually fluctuate, since it is a cellulitis rather than a discrete abscess
The tongue is pushed upward and backward, causing drooling, difficulty swallowing, muffled speech and a serious threat to the airway
Infection is typically polymicrobial with mixed aerobic and anaerobic mouth organisms
The overriding priority is airway management, as swelling can rapidly cause life-threatening obstruction
Treatment combines securing the airway, high-dose intravenous antibiotics and surgical decompression or drainage together with removal of the dental source
Contrast CT delineates the extent of spread and any collection but must never delay airway assessment in a deteriorating patient
reference.pathophysiology: Ludwig angina begins most often as an odontogenic infection of the mandibular molars. Because the roots of the second and third molars lie below the attachment of the mylohyoid muscle, infection spreads into the submandibular space and then communicates with the sublingual and submental spaces, involving all three bilaterally. The result is a rapidly advancing cellulitis of the floor of the mouth with dense inflammatory oedema rather than a localised abscess. Swelling of the sublingual tissues elevates and displaces the tongue posteriorly, while induration of the submandibular region narrows the oropharyngeal airway. Untreated, infection can extend along fascial planes to the parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal spaces and into the mediastinum, and airway obstruction or sepsis can be fatal.
additionalDifferentials: Submandibular sialadenitis or salivary gland abscess
Deep neck space abscess from other sources
Angioedema of the floor of mouth and neck
additionalInvestigations: Early airway assessment and continuous monitoring, taking priority over imaging
Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck to define spread and detect any collection or mediastinal extension
Full blood count, inflammatory markers and blood cultures
Culture and sensitivity of any pus obtained at drainage
Orthopantomogram or dental assessment to identify the causative tooth
Blood glucose and screening for diabetes or immunosuppression
redFlags: Any sign of airway compromise (stridor, drooling, inability to swallow secretions, respiratory distress) constituting an airway emergency
Rapidly progressive neck swelling and inability to protrude the tongue
Features of spreading sepsis, high fever and haemodynamic instability
Chest pain, dyspnoea or widened mediastinum suggesting descending mediastinitis
Trismus limiting mouth opening and airway access
reference.prognosis: With early airway control, prompt intravenous antibiotics and timely surgical drainage the outlook is good, but delay in securing the airway or in treatment can lead to fatal airway obstruction, descending mediastinitis or sepsis.
pitfalls: Underestimating the speed of airway deterioration and delaying definitive airway management
Waiting for fluctuation before intervening, when the process is a cellulitis without a drainable abscess early on
Sending an unstable patient for prolonged imaging instead of prioritising the airway
Overlooking and failing to treat the underlying dental source
Missing spread to the mediastinum in a patient who is not improving
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Prioritise securing the airway, with early anaesthetic and ENT involvement and a low threshold for awake fibreoptic intubation or surgical tracheostomy before obstruction develops
Start empirical intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics covering mouth aerobes and anaerobes, such as a beta-lactam with beta-lactamase-inhibitor combination plus metronidazole, or clindamycin
Undertake urgent surgical incision, drainage and decompression of the involved submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces when there is a collection or airway compromise
Eliminate the source by extracting or treating the causative molar tooth
Provide supportive care with intravenous fluids, analgesia and close monitoring in a high-dependency setting, and control coexisting diabetes or immunosuppression
Watch for and treat spread to the parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal spaces or mediastinum (descending mediastinitis) and evolving sepsis
Escalate to critical care with combined ENT, maxillofacial and anaesthetic management for airway failure or systemic deterioration
